hook_text: The hardest rock on the mountain is being split apart right now, by a drop of water.
clip_script: Rocks look like they last forever. They don't. Right now, on a mountain in the Drakensberg, water is trickling into a crack. Tonight it freezes. Ice takes up more space than water, so it pushes, like a wedge. Tomorrow it melts. Tonight it freezes again. After thousands of nights, the rock splits. That's physical weathering. In a desert, the sun heats rock by day and the night cools it, until its skin peels off like an onion. Meanwhile, rainwater, slightly acidic, dissolves limestone, carving out giant caves like the Cango Caves. That's chemical weathering. And a tiny tree root, growing into a crack, can split a boulder in two. That's biological weathering. Together, these forces turn mountains into soil, and soil feeds us all.
visual_style: Time-lapse style animation of ice forming and widening a crack; a granite dome with peeling layers; dripping water building a stalactite in a cave; a tree root splitting a boulder; a red soil field.
pacing: Slow and rhythmic for freeze and thaw, faster through the other processes.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn the three types of weathering and how climate controls them.
